title: 20th-Century Literature · Novels, voices, and the human condition
summary: Story-first and form-sensitive literary history of forty-seven major twentieth-century works, including landmark sections on Joyce, Proust, Faulkner, Woolf, Borges, Beckett, Eliot, Rushdie, Camus, Nabokov and Hemingway.
assumed_background: No prior reading is required for the story-first lectures, including the Lord of the Rings orientation and complete three-volume narrative.
Analysis lectures assume the preceding complete story orientation or knowledge of the work; specialized Tolkien essays follow the full retelling.
The five Ulysses narrative lectures tell a continuous, spoiler-containing story in order; analytical lectures assume this orientation or prior familiarity with the novel.
The seven Proust story lectures cover the continuous novel volume by volume, with full spoilers; the seven analyses presuppose this orientation or the original work.

The Sound and the Fury has five spoiler-complete narrative orientation lectures followed by seven formal, social, and textual studies; the latter assume the story orientation or knowledge of the novel.
The four To the Lighthouse story lectures cover all three parts and the ending with spoilers; the following eight analyses assume this orientation or independent familiarity with the novel.

The Ficciones section provides complete spoiler-containing story orientations for all seventeen pieces in the expanded edition; seven analyses follow, requiring the story lectures or prior familiarity with the works.

The two Waiting for Godot story lectures contain both acts with spoilers; the following nine analyses assume this orientation or a reading/performance of the play. The play is treated as theatre, not as a novel with a hidden plot resolution.

The Waste Land is a five-part poem, not a single plot: its first six lectures orient listeners to the entire work without assuming prior reading, followed by nine analyses that assume the orientation or access to the poem.

Midnight’s Children has four consecutive, spoiler-complete story lectures from its family prehistory through the 1977 ending. Eight analytic lectures require those or independent knowledge of the novel; historical dates are separated from Saleem’s unreliable claims.

The Stranger has two spoiler-complete narrative lectures covering both parts, followed by seven analyses on form, justice, colonial context, the absurd, translation, reception and close-reading. No prior knowledge of Camus is required for story orientation.

Nabokov’s Lolita has three complete story narrations first, then eight critical lectures. Humbert is a criminal narrator: his characterization of Dolores Haze is not independently authoritative, and John Ray’s foreword is a fictional paratext.

Hemingway’s The Sun Also Rises has three sequential story narrations, followed by seven studies of prose technique, narration, gender, bullfighting, war, history and close reading. The narrator’s account of Robert Cohn requires attention to antisemitism and bias.
